Dear Lalit,

You asked how things are at school, so here it is. I told my class teacher about the name-calling on the 4th. The teacher said, "I'll have a word." Nothing changed, and it got worse in the corridor. I have been writing every incident in a notebook: date, time, place, who saw. My parents read it and wrote a letter to the principal with copies of my pages attached. Three days later the principal called us in with the class teacher and the counsellor. There is a plan now: the boys' seats have been moved, a teacher stands in the corridor at break, and we review on the 20th. It isn't over, but things are moving because we kept pushing calmly. I'll write again after the 20th.

Ganga

qa.q: What did Ganga write in the notebook for every incident?
qa.a: Ganga wrote the date, time, place and who saw.

qa.q: How does Ganga feel about the situation now?
qa.a: Ganga feels cautiously hopeful, saying it isn't over but things are moving because they kept pushing calmly.

qa.q: What could Ganga do if the plan does not work by the 20th, and why?
qa.a: Ganga could go back to the principal with the updated notebook and ask about the next step in the policy, because official channels can escalate when needed.

qa.q: How might Ganga's parents feel about writing to the principal?
qa.a: The parents are probably worried and determined, wanting Ganga protected and willing to press until action is taken.

grounding: When a single teacher conversation changes nothing, the parents write to the principal and the student keeps recording incidents, escalating calmly through official channels until action is taken.

So, Gargi, you want to know what finally worked? It wasn't the first try.

I'm Rehana. In Class 9, two girls kept hiding my books and whispering about my family. I told my class teacher in July. She said she'd "have a word". Nothing changed. For two weeks it was actually worse, because they knew I'd told.

I nearly gave up. But my parents said, "One conversation isn't the end of the road." Abbu helped me keep a notebook: every incident, date, time, who saw.

In August my parents wrote a short, polite letter to the principal, with the notebook pages attached. Within three days we had a meeting with the principal and the counsellor. The girls' parents were called in. The counsellor checked in with me every Friday.

It wasn't dramatic. It was just steady. We kept going up, calmly, until someone acted.

qa.q: When did Rehana first tell the class teacher?
How did Rehana feel when things got worse after telling the teacher?
qa.a: Rehana felt discouraged and close to giving up, because the bullying worsened once the girls knew.

qa.q: What else could the family have done if the principal had not acted?
qa.a: They could have taken the same notebook to the school's management or a child helpline, continuing to escalate calmly through official channels.

qa.q: How might Rehana's parents have seen the first teacher conversation?
qa.a: They probably saw it as a first step that had not worked yet, not a reason to stop, which is why they helped keep the notebook and wrote to the principal.

grounding: A spoken account of parents escalating to the principal when one teacher conversation changed nothing, while the student kept recording incidents until action was taken.

My name's Divyansh. I sit next to Chaitanya in Class 10, and I watched what happened after he complained about the seniors who kept shoving him in the stairwell.

In the first week he talked to our class teacher. She spoke to the seniors. For a few days it stopped. Then it started again, quieter, when no teacher was near.

After that, I noticed Chaitanya writing in a small green notebook at break, every day. Dates, I think. Once I saw the words "3rd floor, 12:40, pushed into railing".

About two weeks later, his father came to school with a letter and went into the principal's office. Chaitanya didn't say much, but the next Monday there was a teacher on the stairwell at every break, and the seniors were called to the office.

I don't know how scared he'd been. But he stopped taking the long way round to class.

qa.q: What words did Divyansh see in the green notebook?
What might Chaitanya have been feeling when the shoving started again?
qa.a: He may have felt frustrated and scared, perhaps let down that the first complaint did not last, which could be why he started keeping the notebook.

qa.q: What would you advise Chaitanya if the stairwell trouble came back?
qa.a: Keep adding to the notebook and tell the principal or counsellor straight away, since the school has already shown it will act on a clear record.

qa.q: How did the whole process look to Divyansh from the next seat?
qa.a: To Divyansh it looked quiet and steady rather than dramatic: a notebook, a letter, and then teachers on the stairwell, though Divyansh cannot know how Chaitanya felt inside.

grounding: An observer's account of a student who kept recording incidents after a first teacher conversation failed, with a parent escalating to the principal until action was taken.
